messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ellen Weiss is a 63-year-old sculptor who came to treatment after years of trying to keep her world narrowed to what she called “the few places that don’t make my skin crawl.” She is married and lives with her husband in a small house where her studio occupies a converted garage, and she now spends most of her days moving between those two rooms. The rape occurred several years ago when someone she knew forced himself on her after an evening gathering. What stayed with Ellen was not only the physical terror but the stunned recognition of the man’s familiarity, the awful collapse of ordinary social trust in the very moment she needed it. She had expected that other people nearby, and later the systems she turned to, would protect her or at least respond with clarity and care. Instead, she experienced the aftermath as another injury. She has come to believe that the people and institutions that should have protected her failed her completely, and that this failure changed something fundamental about how she understands the world.

In the months that followed, certain moments began to hit her with a force that felt out of proportion until she described how directly they brought her back to what happened. A passing siren can stop her in place, especially when she is in her studio with the radio on low and hears it rise suddenly from the street; the sound yanks her into the old conviction that danger is already underway and no one will arrive in time to help. Comments about sexual violence are equally hard for her. If a neighbor mentions an assault case or a television segment touches on rape, Ellen does not hear it as distant news. She feels abruptly flooded with shame and disgust, and the old judgments come roaring back: that she acted in ways that go against who she is, that she somehow failed to protect herself, that the whole event exposed a moral damage in her she cannot undo. Encounters with people connected to that period of her life, even tangentially, are especially potent. Seeing a familiar face from that social circle or hearing someone mention one of those names leaves her feeling again that trust was foolish, that meaning drained out of life the moment those bonds proved false.

Over time, those beliefs hardened into the lens through which she now moves through the day. Ellen is certain that the world is not simply painful but fundamentally unsafe, except in a very limited number of places. Home, and more specifically the studio when the doors are locked, are the only settings where she can exhale at all. Because she has come to believe she was abandoned by the people and institutions that should have protected her, she no longer expects protection from anyone, and that expectation keeps her body tense and watchful. She lives with strong negative feelings that flare quickly—fear, anger, shame, at times horror—while underneath is the deadened conviction that nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore. What frightened her most was not only remembering the rape but the sense that it revealed a permanent truth: that she cannot rely on others, and that some part of her life’s purpose ended there.

That constant sense of danger now shapes what catches her attention and how sharply it lands. When she goes to the supply store for clay or armatures, an unexpected movement beside her—someone reaching across an aisle or stepping out from behind a display—makes her jolt as if she is about to be grabbed. Sirens seem louder when she is already on edge, and she scans immediately for exits, for men nearby, for any sign that she is trapped. Her husband has noticed that if friends suggest dinner out, Ellen first asks who will be there and whether anyone from their old community might appear. The smaller her safe zone has become, the more loaded these cues feel; even the possibility of running into a related person is enough to make her body brace before anything has happened.

This has fed back into the meanings she makes of herself and her life. Each episode of alarm seems to Ellen like proof that the rape still defines her, proof that she has been permanently altered in a way that violates the person she once believed herself to be—open, strong, capable of reading character, able to make art from human experience without feeling contaminated by it. When she startles violently in public or has to leave after overhearing a discussion of sexual assault, she does not read it as a symptom. She takes it as evidence that the damage is deep and enduring, that the institutions failed her so completely there is no repairing what followed, and that the meaningful life she had before has narrowed into mere survival.

What finally brought her in was a recent episode in her studio when a siren passed just as a delivery worker knocked unexpectedly at the side door. Ellen dropped a piece she had been shaping for weeks and could not return to it. She wept afterward, less about the ruined sculpture than about the realization that even the room she depends on for safety no longer reliably feels safe. She is seeking help now because she is afraid her life will keep shrinking until there is nowhere she can go without terror, and because some part of her still hopes that if she can understand why everything feels so dangerous, she might recover not just calm but a sense that her life means something again.
